Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

MOGADISHU, Somalia (CNN)  -- A roadside bombing in Somalia's capital killed 21 women who were cleaning rubbish from a southern Mogadishu street on Sunday morning, a hospital official said. Mogadishu residents gather around victims of the bomb attack along the city's Maka Al Mukarama Road. The bomb blast wounded another 46 people, most of them Somali women who had gathered to clean Maka Al Mukarama Road in southern Mogadishu's Kilometer 4 district, according to Medina Hospital director Dr. Dahir Dhere. "It suddenly turned the area into a carnage, scattering body parts of the street cleaners into a large area," said witness Asha Ise Gedi. "There were pools of blood everywhere. I have never seen such mass killing." "They were innocent poor mothers or sisters," Gedi said. "Why did they deserve this?" It is unclear who is behind the attack. Mogadishu Mayor Mohamed Omar Habeb Mohamed Dhere, who was recently fired by the country's prime minister, blamed the Islamic Courts Union for waging the attack. But the head of the Islamist insurgent group, Abid Rahim Ise Adow, denied any involvement and blamed Somalia's government for orchestrating the attack. The victims were participating in a program that allows Somali women to work as street cleaners in exchange for food. The United Nations' World Food Program organized the program, which began last year and is administered by Mogadishu's regional authority. Mogadishu has been the site of violence in recent months between Ethiopian troops and Islamist fighters. Somalia's current transitional government is trying to maintain control of the capital, with the help of the better-equipped Ethiopian forces. On Saturday, two-thirds of the Somali government ministers announced their resignations, blaming Prime Minister Nur Hassan Nur Ade's "dictatorship," which they said included his firing of Mogadishu's mayor. Nur Ade said he suspects the mass resignations were aimed at weakening implementation of the peace agreement between Somalia's transitional government and the opposition Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia. He said he had no plans to resign. The peace agreement, signed June 9 in Djibouti, calls for a cease-fire between Somalia's U.N.-backed transitional government and the Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia, an opposition group that includes members of the Islamist Court Union which overthrew the government in 2006. The ICU was ousted from power later that year by Ethiopian forces, with the support of Somalia's transitional government. If followed, the peace deal would pave the way for a withdrawal of Ethiopian troops -- a major sticking point for Islamist fighters who oppose their presence. The agreement calls on the alliance to dissociate itself from armed groups still fighting the government and for all sides to allow "unhindered humanitarian access and assistance" to all Somalis. A joint committee led by U.N. officials will monitor the agreement's implementation. Ethiopian forces became embroiled in an Islamist insurgency after the Ethiopian forces invaded Somalia in December 2006 to overthrow the ICU leaders and reinstall the transitional government. As guerrilla attacks mounted, efforts to replace the Ethiopians with an African Union-led peacekeeping mission faltered. Ethiopia's invasion had the blessing of Somalia's government and the United States, which accused the ICU of harboring fugitives from the al Qaeda terrorist movement. The conflict displaced hundreds of thousands of Somalis, further worsening a humanitarian crisis that dates back to the collapse of the country's last government in 1991. The situation has been exacerbated by drought, continual armed conflicts in central and southern Somalia, and high inflation on food and fuel prices. CNN's Alan Duke and journalists Mohamed Amin Adow and Abdi Nasir Mohamed contributed to this report.

**Roadside bombing kills 21 women street cleaners in Mogadishu**

**MOGADISHU, Somalia** — A roadside bomb tore through a group of women working as street cleaners in Somalia’s capital, killing 21 of them and wounding dozens more, witnesses and officials said, in one of the deadliest attacks on civilians in Mogadishu in recent months.

The women were sweeping a street when the device exploded, sending shrapnel through the group and scattering debris across the road. Medical workers said hospitals were struggling to treat the wounded, many of them women who had been earning small daily wages through municipal clean-up work.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the blast.

Mogadishu has been gripped by violence since Somalia’s transitional federal government, backed by Ethiopian troops, drove an Islamist movement from the capital in late 2006. Since then, insurgents have waged a campaign of roadside bombings, mortar attacks and assassinations targeting government officials, Ethiopian forces and their allies. Civilians have often borne the brunt of the fighting.

Somalia’s transitional government, established with international backing after years of civil war and lawlessness, has struggled to exert authority beyond parts of Mogadishu and a few other areas. The government depends heavily on Ethiopian military support, a presence that has fueled resentment among many Somalis and become a rallying point for Islamist insurgent groups.

Those insurgents include remnants of the Islamic Courts Union, which briefly controlled Mogadishu and much of southern Somalia before being ousted by Ethiopian and government forces. More hardline factions have rejected negotiations and continued attacks, saying they will fight until Ethiopian troops leave the country.

The bombing comes despite a peace agreement signed in Djibouti between Somalia’s transitional government and a faction of the opposition. The Djibouti accord called for a cease-fire, the withdrawal of Ethiopian forces under certain conditions, and the deployment of international peacekeepers. But key insurgent factions dismissed the agreement, and violence has continued across the capital.

Residents said the latest attack underscored the dangers faced by ordinary Somalis trying to survive amid the conflict.

“These women were not soldiers,” one witness said. “They were just cleaning the road to feed their families.”

Somalia has had no fully functioning central government since 1991, when the overthrow of dictator Mohamed Siad Barre plunged the country into clan warfare, warlord rule and repeated humanitarian crises. International efforts to stabilize the country have repeatedly faltered as rival political factions, clan militias and Islamist fighters compete for power.

**Roadside blast kills women street cleaners in Somalia’s capital amid widening insurgency**

**MOGADISHU, Somalia —** A roadside bomb exploded in Somalia’s capital, Mogadishu, killing a group of poor women who had been sweeping streets as part of a municipal cleaning effort, witnesses and local officials said. The victims were among the city’s most vulnerable residents: women earning small daily wages clearing rubbish from roads scarred by years of war.

The blast struck as the cleaners worked along a roadside in the capital, an area frequently targeted by insurgents with improvised explosive devices aimed at government officials, Ethiopian troops, or African Union peacekeepers. Instead, the explosion tore through civilians.

Witnesses described scenes of panic as bystanders rushed to help the wounded. “They were only cleaning the street,” one resident said. “They had no weapons. They were poor women trying to earn money for their families.”

No group immediately claimed responsibility. In Mogadishu, however, roadside bombs, assassinations, mortar attacks, and ambushes have become hallmarks of the insurgency against Somalia’s internationally backed transitional government and its foreign military allies.

Local authorities condemned the attack as an act of terror against civilians. The deaths underscored the brutal reality of Somalia’s conflict: even basic public work—cleaning roads, reopening markets, repairing infrastructure—can become deadly in a city where front lines shift, armed groups operate in crowded neighborhoods, and explosive devices are often planted along busy routes.

## A capital caught between government, insurgents, and foreign forces

The blast occurred against the backdrop of Somalia’s long-running political and military crisis. The country has lacked a strong central government since the fall of dictator Mohamed Siad Barre in 1991, after which warlords, clan militias, Islamist movements, and foreign-backed authorities competed for power.

At the center of the current conflict is Somalia’s **Transitional Federal Government**, or TFG, a weak but internationally recognized administration created through peace talks and supported by the United Nations, the African Union, Ethiopia, the United States, and other foreign partners. The TFG has struggled to exert authority beyond parts of Mogadishu and a few other areas, relying heavily on foreign military support.

Opposing it are Islamist insurgent groups, including remnants of the **Islamic Courts Union** and more militant factions such as **al-Shabab**, which emerged as one of the most powerful armed movements in the country. These groups portray the transitional government as illegitimate and accuse it of being a puppet of foreign powers, especially Ethiopia.

## Ethiopia’s intervention and the insurgency

Ethiopia, Somalia’s powerful western neighbor, intervened militarily in Somalia in late 2006 to help the transitional government oust the Islamic Courts Union, which had taken control of Mogadishu and much of southern Somalia. Ethiopia argued that Islamist forces posed a threat to its security, particularly because some Somali Islamist leaders had voiced support for claims over Ethiopia’s Somali-inhabited Ogaden region.

The Ethiopian intervention succeeded in removing the Islamic Courts administration from power, but it also triggered a fierce insurgency. Many Somalis, including some who did not support hardline Islamist rule, viewed Ethiopian troops as occupiers. That resentment helped insurgent groups recruit fighters and gain local support.

Since then, Mogadishu has seen repeated cycles of violence: insurgents plant roadside bombs and launch hit-and-run attacks; Ethiopian and government forces respond with raids, artillery, and security sweeps; civilians are caught in the middle.

Human rights groups have repeatedly warned that all sides have contributed to civilian suffering. Insurgent attacks often take place in crowded areas, while government and allied forces have been accused of indiscriminate responses that kill or displace noncombatants.

## The African Union’s difficult mission

The **African Union** deployed a peacekeeping force to Somalia, known as **AMISOM**, to support the transitional government and help stabilize Mogadishu. Troops from countries including Uganda and Burundi were sent into one of the world’s most dangerous urban battlefields.

AMISOM’s mandate included protecting key government sites, the airport, seaport, and presidential compound, as well as helping create conditions for humanitarian aid and political reconciliation. But the force was under-resourced, deployed in limited numbers, and frequently targeted by insurgents.

For many Somalis, the AU presence was seen as less provocative than Ethiopia’s, but Islamist opposition groups still denounced AMISOM as a foreign occupation force. AU troops have been attacked with mortars, suicide bombings, roadside bombs, and ambushes.

## The United Nations and the search for a political settlement

The **United Nations** has backed Somalia’s transitional institutions and repeatedly called for reconciliation among Somali factions. UN officials have urged political dialogue, humanitarian access, and the withdrawal or replacement of foreign forces under a broader peace arrangement.

The UN has also warned that Somalia’s conflict is not only a military crisis but a humanitarian catastrophe. Fighting in Mogadishu has displaced hundreds of thousands of people, many of whom fled to makeshift camps with little access to clean water, food, or medical care. Civilians face overlapping threats: war, famine risk, disease, piracy along the coast, and the collapse of public services.

International diplomats have tried to encourage talks between the transitional government and more moderate Islamist opposition figures, arguing that a purely military solution is unlikely. But negotiations have been complicated by deep clan divisions, mistrust of Ethiopia, competition among Islamist factions, and the rise of hardliners who reject compromise.

## Civilians pay the highest price

The deaths of the women street cleaners highlight the human cost of Somalia’s war. In a city where unemployment is widespread and many families depend on informal labor, street cleaning can provide one of the few sources of income for poor women. Their work is also symbolic: an attempt to restore normal life in a capital repeatedly devastated by conflict.

Instead, the roadside blast showed how far Mogadishu remains from stability. Bombs meant to undermine the government or attack foreign troops often kill the very civilians that all sides claim to defend.

For residents, the attack was another reminder that in Somalia’s capital, danger is woven into ordinary life—waiting at a market, riding a minibus, walking to work, or sweeping a street.
